how: Multiply length by width by thickness. Keep all dimensions in the same unit.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft slab that is 0.5 ft thick needs 100 cubic feet of concrete.
tips: Measure the actual thickness at several points.
Add a project-specific allowance for waste or uneven ground.

how: Divide the required concrete volume by the yield of one bag, then round up to a whole bag.
example: If a project needs 10 cubic feet and each bag yields 0.6 cubic feet, you need 17 bags.
tips: Use the yield printed on the exact bag product.
Buy enough bags to avoid a shortage during placement.

how: Multiply length by width by depth. Use consistent units for every measurement.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft area with 0.25 ft of gravel needs 50 cubic feet before any allowance.
tips: Depth should represent the planned compacted or installed layer as appropriate.
Ask the supplier whether their quoted quantity is loose or compacted.

how: Multiply the garden area dimensions by the planned mulch depth.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft bed with a 0.25 ft depth needs 50 cubic feet of mulch.
tips: Confirm the depth recommended for the type of mulch you use.
Account for settling if appropriate to the product.

how: Divide wall area by product coverage and multiply by the number of coats.
example: For 800 square feet, 350 square feet of coverage per unit and two coats, the estimate is 4.57 units.
tips: Use the manufacturer's stated coverage for your specific product.
Porous or rough surfaces can require more material.

how: Multiply length by width to get area, then add the selected waste percentage.
example: A 20 ft by 15 ft room is 300 square feet. With 10% waste, plan for 330 square feet.
tips: Follow the flooring manufacturer's installation guidance for waste.
Irregular rooms and complex patterns may need a higher allowance.

how: Divide the total area by the area of one tile, add the waste percentage, then round up.
example: For 1,000 square feet using 12 by 12 inch tiles with 10% waste, the estimate is 92 tiles.
tips: Use actual tile dimensions when they differ from nominal dimensions.
Keep spare tiles for future repairs when practical.

how: Estimate wall surface area from room dimensions and divide by the area of one sheet, then round up.
example: A rectangular room with 20 ft length, 15 ft width and 8 ft walls has 560 square feet of wall area before deductions.
tips: This basic calculator does not subtract doors or windows.
Ceilings, openings, layout, and local installation practices can change the final quantity.

how: Calculate board feet as thickness in inches multiplied by width in inches multiplied by length in feet, divided by 12, then multiply by quantity.
example: A 2 by 6 board that is 8 ft long contains 8 board feet.
tips: Use actual dimensions when pricing rough or surfaced lumber.
Supplier pricing may use different grading and measurement conventions.

how: Multiply quantity by unit price and then add the selected waste percentage.
example: 100 units at $4 each with 10% waste gives an estimated total of $440.
tips: Use the current price for the exact product and unit.
Taxes, delivery, labor and other project costs are not included unless added separately.

how: Multiply the paved area by 144 to convert square feet to square inches, divide by the paver area, add waste, then round up.
example: A 20 ft by 12 ft patio using 12 by 6 inch pavers with 5% waste needs about 504 pavers.
tips: Use the actual paver dimensions.
Patterns and cutting can change the waste requirement.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft area with a 0.1 ft layer needs 20 cubic feet.
tips: Confirm the planned layer depth and whether the supplier sells loose or compacted material.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 10 ft by 10 ft bed with a 0.5 ft depth needs 50 cubic feet of soil.
tips: Account for settling and the finished grade when choosing an order quantity.

how: Convert fence length to inches and divide by the picket width plus the gap, then round up.
example: A 100 ft fence with 5.5 inch pickets and a 1.5 inch gap needs 172 pickets in this simplified straight-run calculation.
tips: Check the actual picket width and desired spacing before ordering.

how: Divide fence length by planned post spacing, round up, then add one post for the starting position.
example: A 100 ft fence at 8 ft spacing requires 14 posts.
tips: Corners, gates and ends can require additional posts.

how: Estimate the number of board rows from deck width and board width plus gap, then divide the deck length by board length and add waste.
example: A 12 ft by 20 ft deck using 6 inch boards, a 0.125 inch gap and 12 ft boards needs 48 boards before waste in this simplified row calculation.
tips: Joins, overhangs, picture framing and board lengths can change the actual quantity.

how: Divide roof surface area in square feet by 100.
example: A 2,400 square foot roof surface equals 24 roofing squares.
tips: Use measured roof surface area when available. A roofing square is 100 square feet.

how: Multiply roof area by one plus the selected waste percentage.
example: A 2,400 square foot roof with 10% waste gives 2,640 square feet of estimated material.
tips: Product coverage and installation details vary by roofing system.

how: Multiply volume by the bulk density expressed in compatible units.
example: If 10 cubic units of gravel have a bulk density of 1.6 weight units per cubic unit, the estimate is 16 weight units.
tips: Use the supplier's stated density for the specific material.

how: Multiply concrete volume by the density expressed in compatible units.
example: If 10 cubic units of concrete have a density of 150 weight units per cubic unit, the estimate is 1,500 weight units.
tips: Use a density compatible with the volume units you entered.

how: Multiply length, width and depth using the same unit for all dimensions.
example: A 20 by 1 by 0.5 unit footing has a volume of 10 cubic units.
tips: Use the planned footing dimensions from the project design.
Add allowances only when appropriate to the project.

how: Multiply the number of bars by the length of each bar.
example: 20 bars at 4 units each require 80 length units.
tips: This is a length estimate and does not account for laps, hooks or cutting.
Use the bar schedule for final ordering.

how: Divide required gravel volume by the coverage of one bag and round up.
example: 10 cubic units divided by 0.5 cubic units per bag requires 20 bags.
tips: Use the actual bag coverage printed by the supplier.
Account for compaction where relevant.

how: Divide total measured baseboard length by the length of one piece and round up.
example: 100 units divided by 8 units per piece requires 13 pieces.
tips: Measure around the actual room perimeter.
Subtract openings only when they will not receive baseboard.

how: Divide wall area by the coverage of one roll and round up.
example: 120 square units divided by 25 square units per roll requires 5 rolls.
tips: Use the manufacturer's coverage and pattern information.
Pattern repeats and waste can increase the required rolls.

how: Divide total vertical rise by the planned riser height and round up.
example: A 96 unit total rise at 8 units per riser gives 12 risers.
tips: Use the final stair design for code-compliant dimensions.
This is a quantity estimate, not a stair design tool.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 20 by 10 area at 0.2 depth requires 40 cubic units of asphalt.
tips: Use the planned compacted depth where appropriate.
Supplier conversion and density may be needed for ordering by weight.

how: Multiply length, width and depth, then divide cubic feet by 27 when the inputs are in feet.
example: A 27 by 1 by 1 foot volume equals 1 cubic yard.
tips: Use feet for all three inputs when using this conversion.
For ordering, confirm supplier conventions and compaction.

how: Multiply length by width using the same unit for both measurements.
example: A 20 by 15 rectangle has an area of 300 square units.
tips: Use the actual finished dimensions.
Irregular areas may need to be split into multiple rectangles.

how: Multiply length by width by height using consistent units.
example: A 20 by 15 by 2 rectangular volume is 600 cubic units.
tips: This tool assumes a rectangular shape.
Use consistent units for all dimensions.
